papers.title: Learning with Recurrence Geometric AI in Spatial Transcriptomics
papers.summary: This paper appears to propose a new AI method that combines recurrent neural network architectures with geometric deep learning principles to analyze spatial transcriptomics data. The abstract title suggests the approach captures both sequential/iterative patterns and geometric relationships in spatial gene expression data, though technical details are minimal. Without more information, it seems to be a methods-focused paper introducing a novel computational framework for this data type.
papers.why: Advanced AI methods for spatial transcriptomics could directly enhance analysis of gene expression patterns in interneurons and perineuronal nets within brain tissue, supporting the spatial transcriptomics component of this mitophagy research.

papers.title: Morphodynamic domains enable integration of live morphometrics and spatial transcriptomics
papers.summary: This paper introduces a computational method called 'morphodynamic domains' that captures how cell shapes change over time using live imaging. It then integrates these dynamic morphological features with spatial transcriptomics data, linking cell shape behavior to gene expression patterns in tissue context. This creates a framework for connecting live-cell dynamics with fixed spatial molecular data.
papers.why: This method could offer a new way to link live imaging-based morphometrics with spatial transcriptomics, which is directly relevant to studying dynamic processes like autophagy/mitophagy in neurons alongside spatially resolved molecular profiling.

papers.title: Highly Sensitive Spatial Host-Microbiome Transcriptomics in FFPE Tissues via Iterative Hydrogel Expansion.
papers.summary: This paper presents a method for spatial host-microbiome transcriptomics in formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) tissues using iterative hydrogel expansion. The technique increases sensitivity for detecting both host and microbial RNA transcripts while preserving their spatial location in tissue sections. This allows researchers to study interactions between host cells and microbial communities directly within their native tissue context at improved resolution.
papers.why: While focused on microbiome-host interactions rather than neurons, the underlying iterative hydrogel expansion technique for spatial transcriptomics in FFPE tissue could offer methodological insights for improving resolution and sensitivity in spatial transcriptomic analyses of brain tissue relevant to this PhD project.
papers.figure: A figure showing the workflow of iterative hydrogel expansion applied to FFPE tissue sections, alongside spatial transcript detection sensitivity comparisons before and after expansion.

papers.title: Post-translational Regulation of the PI3K/Akt/mTOR–Autophagy Axis in Osteoblast Differentiation and Its Polypharmacological Targeting by Eupolyphaga sinensis
papers.summary: This paper studies how the PI3K/Akt/mTOR signaling pathway controls autophagy during osteoblast (bone-forming cell) differentiation, focusing on modifications that occur after proteins are made (post-translational regulation). It also examines how a traditional medicine ingredient, Eupolyphaga sinensis, acts on multiple targets within this pathway to influence bone cell development. The work combines molecular biology and pharmacology to map how this insect-derived compound might therapeutically modulate autophagy-related bone formation processes.
papers.why: Although focused on bone biology rather than neurons, this paper's detailed mechanistic dissection of PI3K/Akt/mTOR-autophagy pathway regulation could offer transferable insights into autophagy/mitophagy signaling relevant to neuronal and interneuron studies.
papers.figure: A pathway diagram illustrating the post-translational modifications (e.g., phosphorylation, ubiquitination) of PI3K/Akt/mTOR components and their downstream effects on autophagy machinery.

papers.title: Transcriptome-based macroautophagy and chaperone-mediated autophagy states reveal context-dependent vulnerabilities across human cancers.
papers.summary: This paper develops a way to score tumor samples for macroautophagy and chaperone-mediated autophagy activity purely from transcriptome data. Using these scores, the authors classify cancers into different autophagy 'states' and link these states to specific molecular and clinical vulnerabilities. The approach suggests that autophagy pathway activity varies widely by cancer context and could inform targeted therapeutic strategies.
papers.why: Although focused on cancer, this paper's transcriptome-based scoring method for macroautophagy and chaperone-mediated autophagy offers a transferable analytical framework that could be adapted to classify autophagy/mitophagy states in neuronal spatial transcriptomics data.

papers.title: Inhibition of the PTBP1-PRKCZ axis activates autophagy to reprogram bone marrow mesenchymal stem cell fate commitment and ameliorate osteoporosis.
papers.summary: This study looks at bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells and how their fate—whether they become bone-forming or fat-forming cells—can be shifted by blocking a molecular pathway called PTBP1-PRKCZ. Blocking this pathway turns on autophagy, a cellular recycling process, which pushes stem cells toward bone formation instead of fat formation. This reprogramming helps reduce osteoporosis symptoms, at least in the model system studied.
papers.why: While this paper focuses on bone stem cells rather than neurons, the core mechanism—autophagy activation reprogramming cell fate—may offer conceptual parallels for how autophagy/mitophagy pathways influence cell state and function in neurons or glia relevant to your work.
papers.figure: A figure showing the effect of PTBP1-PRKCZ inhibition on autophagy markers and osteogenic vs adipogenic differentiation outcomes in bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells.

papers.title: TOLLIP suppresses picornavirus internalization by targeting and degrading VP1 protein through selective autophagy.
papers.summary: This study finds that a protein called TOLLIP helps cells defend against picornaviruses (a family of small viruses) by targeting the viral VP1 protein for destruction. This degradation happens through selective autophagy, a process where cells tag specific unwanted proteins and send them to be broken down. As a result, TOLLIP blocks the virus from being taken up into cells, reducing infection.
papers.why: Although focused on viral infection rather than neurons, this paper is relevant because it details molecular mechanisms of selective autophagy targeting a specific protein for degradation, which parallels the selective autophagy pathways (like mitophagy) central to your PhD research on neuronal quality control.
papers.figure: A figure showing the proposed mechanism/pathway of TOLLIP-mediated selective autophagy and degradation of VP1 protein.

papers.title: Glucocorticoids Impair the Airway Epithelial Barrier via Autophagy-Associated Apoptosis in Asthma: A Preliminary Study Both In Vitro and In Vivo.
papers.summary: This study investigates how glucocorticoid drugs, commonly used to treat asthma, can paradoxically damage the airway's protective epithelial barrier. Using both cell culture and animal models, the researchers found that glucocorticoids trigger a form of programmed cell death linked to autophagy, a cellular self-digestion process. This suggests a potential downside to long-term glucocorticoid use in asthma treatment, as it may weaken rather than strengthen airway defenses.
papers.why: While focused on airway epithelium rather than neurons, this paper's mechanistic insights into autophagy-associated apoptosis could inform analogous investigations of autophagy dysregulation in neuronal or glial cell death within the brain.
papers.figure: A figure showing autophagy marker expression (e.g., LC3-II, p62) alongside apoptosis markers and barrier integrity measurements (e.g., TEER or tight junction protein staining) in glucocorticoid-treated epithelial cells versus controls.
